comments.text:
Brett Adcock and Garry Tan are right that traditional tech interviews are breaking in the AI era, and that's good. 

But the problem is bigger than building a post AI LeetCode. So, here are a few thoughts:

In fast moving areas, static challenges decay quickly. Even a 30 question test like Brett’s will lose predictive power as agents evolve. A document review like Garry suggests is closer to real work, but without benchmarking and test security, it is hard to compare candidates fairly.

There are a few simple truths:
- If everyone aces it, or everyone fails it, the test is broken. You have to keep adjusting it as the world changes. There are now ways to build self-healing tests, like what one of the teams at Workera does.
- If the job is only about using AI well, let candidates use AI. If it is about other skills, test those the right way. Not everything should be open book. Use close book when it makes sense.
- If two great candidates produce different but good answers, you still need a fair way to compare them.

So yes, Brett is right that something new is needed. Garry is right that agent use must be embraced. But the opp is not just a new question bank. It is a dynamic, continuously validated measurement layer for the AI era.

text:
I spoke to the Head of Finance for a Series B tech startup yesterday.

He did a full AI show-and-tell & by the end it felt like he was going to bust through the screen like the Kool-Aid man. 

Some highlights from the call:

1. The first problem he attacked with AI was building a financial operating model for investors to raise their next round of funding.

His process: Uploaded data room context from previous fundraise, had Claude ask clarifying questions, then iteratively built ARR waterfall and expense budget. 

He said he finished the model in 2 hours vs 1-2 weeks (without AI).

2. The next problem he tackled was on the customer success side. 

He built a dashboard for clients that tracks incremental revenue (reported by customers), contract cost, and ROI. 

He also made an internal version of this dashboard that notifies customer success when ROI dips below a certain threshold.

3. He took the ROI dashboard one step further and added a function that exports key metrics and charts from a customers dashboard into a brand-aligned QBR deck that is comprehensive and editable.

4. He brought up this concept of the AI stack I can’t stop thinking about. 

Traditionally, when you hire an executive, you don’t just hire them for their qualifications. You also hire them for their network, playbooks, and vendor preferences. 

The same thing will happen for ALL employees. When you hire someone in the future, you’ll hire them for their AI stack (their internal tools, workflows, and skills), which gives them leverage and edge.

5. He believes the painstaking task of month end close for a company’s financials can be taken from 10 days to 1 day with the right AI systems.

6. Every knowledge worker is turning into an engineer, and the way every knowledge worker approaches their work will look like the software lifecycle. 

This guy talked about his approach to building financial models with Claude, and it sounded exactly how my engineers build software. 

Context dump -> PRD -> master plan -> orchestrate/execute -> iterate 

7. The best way to rebuild your company processes to be AI-native is NOT to ask employees for problems. It’s audit everything they do. 

Sit behind them as they work. Take a fine tooth comb to their calendar. Have them walk you through their most common workflows. 

8. Final project: he built a compensation management system by using Google Sheets app script macros generated by Claude Code. 

Its capabilities include system pulls from Rippling API and financial model for scenario planning, auto-generated presentation slides with compensation philosophy and individual comp details, and leveling band validation (flags out-of-band compensation. 

P.S. I spend half of my week talking to execs about how they use AI in their business. 

If you’re an exec and you’re afraid your company isn’t doing enough with AI, shoot me an email and my team will help create a list of clear AI opportunities specific to your business.

text:
I thought AEO (read: SEO for LLMs) was a hunk of bullsh*t. 

And then i spoke to Kipp Bodnar, CMO of HubSpot, who knocked the skepticism out of me. 

His first jab: In one year, they grew AI search traffic by 15x. It went from rounding error to real line item on the P&L.

His second jab: AI search conversion rates are 5x higher than Google search. On some queries, 13x higher.

His hook: 60% of AI citations don't come from the top 20 Google results. The companies dominating Google aren't automatically winning in AI search, which creates a huge advantage for early adopters. 

He then took me through his process for crushing AEO & seeing results in days, not months (like SEO): 

1) Grade: your current AEO presence across ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Gemini with a tool like Hubspot's AEO grader. 

2) Restructure: your content into chunked, answer-first pages with natural language headers. 
- one consolidated page, not 8-10 interlinked pages
- lead with natural language questions like "What is X?"
- 1-2 paragraph sections, not 1,000 word sections
- table of contents on a single page

3) Separate: Mentions from citations and optimize differently for each
- Mention = when AI references your brand or product in its answer but doesn't link to you
- Citation = when an AI references you AND links to your page

4) Open up: your information — ungate content, build Reddit presence, make pricing public
- Optimize for entity understanding: how well do AI models understand what your company does, based on every signal from Reddit to review sites, awards lists to help docs

5) Tool up: with AEO-specific software to track prompts and share of voice
- Check out Xfunnel or Limey[.]ai

6) Rethink attribution: measure source of customers, not source of traffic. 
- Metrics that matter: share of voice, citation count, sentiment, mention frequency, source of customers not traffic

Check out our full convo about AEO below 👇

comments.text:
First, grading and restructuring content is tactical optimisation. It improves eligibility for citation. It doesn't measure whether your brand survives through multi turn narrowing. Being cited in turn one is not the same as being selected in turn four.
Second, the “60% of citations don’t come from top 20 Google results” point is a structural shift, but it cuts both ways. It creates opportunity for early movers, yes. It also increases volatility. Model updates can reweight sources overnight. Without baseline measurement at final recommendation stage, you can't tell whether gains are durable or temporary.

RE #5: we've found this isn't the best tactic for consumer brands hoping to get their products into the agentic purchase funnel now being built in ChatGPT and Gemini. Share of voice is a brand metric so it won't tell if your SKU is being recommended and therefore eligible for purchase. It's important to track whether each of your products are being selected and recommended in the conversations you want to be in. But tracking prompts for commerce is also a slippery slope because LLMs map queries to points in a high-dimensional vector space. 1,000 different prompts can map to the exact same point. By optimizing for a stable intent cluster (e.g. the product category you want your product surfaced in), you become the "nearest neighbor" for an infinite long-tail of queries. Tracking 5,000 prompts is simply measuring the same mathematical point 5,000 times.

text:
I’m convinced that agencies and service businesses will never be the same.

I spoke to the owner of a $10m accounting firm today and he’s rebuilding his business from the ground up.

The highlights from our convo:

1. The first AI agent they built is for handling accounts payable (AP) because it is the most manual and repeatable, least complex workflow in his business.

2. The financial impact of this agent is wild. The firm had a $7 cost per invoice (read: labor costs to process AP) before the agent. Now? $0.20.

3. So many vertical-specific AI startups fail because they lack subject matter expertise in the specific domain they’re trying to disrupt. 

4. The most dangerous knowledge workers/execs are those that live at the intersection of product thinking, AI literate, and deep subject matter expertise.

5. Getting an AI agent to be 80% accurate took him 1 week. Getting it to be 98% accurate took 6 months. People underestimate how long it takes to feed AI every edge case & tweak needed to make it more performant than a human.

6. He’s considering raising $ for the AI AP agent. I think service business owners with the product sensibility to commercialize internal AI tools are a great opportunity for VCs.

7. AI agents don’t have to just be better than their human counterparts. They have to be orders of magnitude better. Because we tend to overestimate the skill of our species and underestimate the skill of technology. 

8. The last job accountants/accounting firms will have is as high-level orchestrator of agents and triager of tier 1 problems flagged by your agents.

9. The AP AI agent was built by him and another non-technical accountant in the business. They used Cursor + Claude Code exclusively. 

P.S. I spend half of my week talking to execs about how they use AI in their business. 

If you’re an exec and you’re afraid your company isn’t doing enough with AI, shoot me an email and my team will help create a list of clear AI opportunities specific to your business. 

alex@tenex[.]co

Together, we are going to enable the biggest companies in the world to build production-ready, complex & secure systems—especially enterprise-ready software including internal tools. 

Tenex will bring deep engineering expertise to productionize complex backend systems, while Lovable enables teams to ship intuitive, flexible frontends faster than ever.

text:
People I deeply respect have called me crazy for every business I've started. 

At Morning Brew, it was "how do you expect to build a REAL business on a newsletter?" 
Now, at Tenex, it's "are you out of your mind starting a dev shop?"

The skepticism was palpable: 

- "Dev shops have a horrific reputation." 
- "You'll never be able to attract great talent." 
- "Companies don't want to work with dev shops." 
- "Dev shops create sloppy software with underpaid talent." 

We heard them, but where they saw red flags, we saw massive upside. 

Misbranding is one of the greatest arbitrages in business & we saw that so clearly in front of us. 

"What if we change the story around dev shops?"

From something a CEO/COO/CTO wouldn't touch with a 10ft pole to THE ONLY WAY to access top .1% AI engineering talent in the U.S. 

Our thesis was simple: 

If we offer engineers uncapped upside (aka paid like salespeople) & the opportunity to gain mastery over building with AI & building AI systems for customers, we think we can pull it off. 

Usually it takes bets like this years to pay off, but given how fast things are moving, the thesis has played out in just 11 months. 

1) We have the best engineers I've ever worked with in my life. Engineers I would never have been able to hire in my previous businesses. 

2) We have unbelievable companies from hockey-stick growth Series B startups to $250bn Fortune 50 companies working with our "dev shop" to access talent/expertise they couldn't on their own. 

We unf*cked a bad brand & it's paying off big time.

text:
11 observations interviewing 500+ engineers the last 9 months: 

1) The new H1B visa thing is a big bummer. We have to say no to lots of qualified candidates because it's financially irresponsible for us to spend $100,000 extra to hire someone. 

2) There are very few true full-stack engineers out there. Most applicants are 90% backend or 90% devops or 90% data eng with a splash of full-stack. Being a true five-tool hitter has never been more important. 

3) The spread in compensation ranges is wild. I'll have one call with a Series C senior engineer making $600k/yr, then I'll have a second call with a SWEII at Microsoft making $175k/yr. Comp is all over the map and a moving target. 

4) The biggest risk with big tech engineers is lack of experience building systems end-to-end. Technical depth may be really strong, but ability to own & system is iffy. 

5) There are very few AI-native engineers. An AI-native engineer is someone that has completely rearchitected their personal workflows for building software. To be AI-native, your process should be >75% different than pre-AI. 

6) There are very few AI engineers. An AI engineer is someone that has built and deployed production agentic systems (ideally at scale). Because the technology is so new, you either have to find a diamond in the rough or hire someone you think can learn fast. 

7) Strong communication is rare as hell & when you find it, it's glorious. All of our engineers at Tenex are client-facing, but outside of that strong communicators are usually strong thinkers and strong thinking has never been more important in engineering. 

8) Testing an engineer's technical chops has never been harder. When everything is Claude Code-able, quickly understanding an engineers fundamental systems & engineering abilities is very hard. Someone will make a billion dollars solving this problem. 

9) Great engineers under-estimate themselves. Mediocre engineers over-estimate themselves. I always ask the question: "If you had to rank yourself 0-10 as an engineer, what number would you pick & why?" The best engineers I've hired give themselves a 7.5/10 max. 

10) Engineers are way more interested in being influencers/creators than I ever imagined. Part of the reason they're interested in joining us is they want to be the next Theo Browne or Michael Primeason. 

11) There are two types of engineers: those who view it as a job and those who view it as a craft. Those who view it as a craft are typically more entrepreneurial, are always cooking up a weekend side project, and view engineering as a core part of their identity.

text:
Today, a senior exec at a multi-billion dollar talent agency told me that he found Tenex by asking Grok for the best AI transformation firms, not Google. Grok.

This isn't a one-off anymore. The frequency of prospects finding us through LLMs is just taking off, and traditional SEO traffic is moving in the exact opposite direction.

Here's what most CMOs are missing: Ranking number one on Google doesn't mean anything anymore. It's about whether ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Gemini can accurately explain what your company does when someone asks.

60% of AI answers cite the wrong source or straight up misrepresent your brand. Your SEO might be dialed, but if AI cannot parse your site, you are invisible in the conversations where decisions now start.

This is Answer Engine Optimization or AEO, and it is the next battleground.

Three things that matter for AEO:

- Structure over keywords. LLMs need clean semantic HTML and schema markup.

- Clarity over cleverness. Vague marketing copy confuses AI; direct claims get cited.

- Speed and reliability. If your site is slow or breaks, AI deprioritizes you.

I've been digging into how Webflow approaches this. Their sites auto-generate the technical stuff that LLMs need: semantic code, schema markup, even LLM's .text files, with no plugins and no dev bottleneck. 

If you're a CMO and you are still optimizing purely for Google rankings, you are going the way of the dinosaurs.

Check out more about Webflow here: https://wfl.io/4rhKM9s

text:
Was just talking to the CEO of a $10m medical supplies business. 

He said insurance documentation & reimbursement costs him $200k in labor costs per year. 

He wants to use AI to streamline the process, but he's worried...

"There are literally dozens of AI tools solving this exact problem...I don'tf know if they're actually good...and they want to lock me into a 12-month contract." 

I'm hearing this problem over & over from founders & execs. 

They are all in on AI. 
They want to use the technology to create leverage in their business. 

But they don't know what is/isn't vaporware and being locked into 6-figure contracts with no out is hard to stomach. 

For AI-interested execs: 
- don't lock yourself into lengthy contracts before validating the product
- you have more leverage than ever before in a sea of software
- talk to active customers
- always weigh build vs. buy before pulling trigger

For AI startups: 
- plz don't sell snake oil. it ruins the party for everyone.
- offering shorter starting contracts, while letting your product do the talking is a great way to stand out.

The reason that AEO playbook felt "trash" to Kipp is likely positioning.
AEO (Account-Based Everything) is a system designed for a specific buyer profile and value prop.
Most creators apply AEO frameworks to their positioning before they've answered:
→ Who is my true ICP?
→ What problem am I solving *for them*?
→ Why should they trust me?
Without clear positioning, AEO becomes just another tactic that feels forced.
What I've seen work:
Build positioning first (clarity on who + problem + unique angle)
→ Then layer in AEO tactics (personalization, intent signals, routing)
Reverse the order? It feels inauthentic and metrics tank.
Kipp's probably seeing creators use AEO tactics without the positioning foundation. That's the trash part.

text:
McKinsey surveyed 2,000 companies in 2025. A whopping 51% said AI backfired on them. Top reason?

Inaccuracy.

From what I can tell, most of these systems weren't broken. They were unreliable. And unreliable is wayyyy worse because you can't predict when it fails.

So I got Ashalesh Tilawat (the Mr. Miyagi of teaching AI) from Gauntlet AI to walk me through the solution. 

Here's his 2026 framework for evaluating if your AI is trustworthy, reliable, and production-ready:

1. build your golden set
Identify 30–50 core requests your AI must handle correctly. The stuff that, if broken, makes the whole system useless. And sit with the person whose job this AI is doing/automating/replacing/helping with. 

2. test the weird stuff
Your golden set covers common requests. But in production, users don't only ask common requests. So build a matrix of categories (topic x complexity) and fill the gaps. Every gap is a corner where failures can hide behind. 

3. build a replay harness
Record the exact state of every interaction so you can test prompt changes without burning API calls. Think of it like game film... you don't put players back on the field just to review the play.

4. create your rubric
Use an LLM to grade outputs on accuracy, completeness, and tone. But calibrate it first -> run 50–100 examples through human and LLM scoring, find disagreements, fix the rubric, repeat until they match.

5. run experiments
New model? Prompt rewrite? Run your eval suite against both versions. Ship if the golden set passes, no regressions, and the cost is acceptable. 

The teams still running production AI on vibes will be f***** in 2026. 

But the teams building eval libraries are compounding an advantage that gets harder to catch every month. Competitors can copy your product. They can't copy your test cases.

h/t Austen Allred for helping put this together.

text:
We founded Morning Brew on a set of principles. 

Those principles have evolved, but they've never been more important. 

In a post-AI world, trusted distribution is one of the final moats.

Here are the 12 rules of the media game as I see them today:

Rule #1: Personality-driven content is becoming a bigger part of media diets.
- The democratization of creation & distribution (read: internet & social platforms) means that people can attract as much distribution as institutions. 

Rule #2: Brand-driven content isn’t dead. 
- Personality-driven content is a necessity for most media brands today, but with it comes a lot of risk. One of the ways to derisk personality risk is by having faceless franchises that give you ownership over a healthy % of your audience.

Rule #3: Riches are in the niches.
- In a world of unlimited choice, consumers can find great content related to any/all interests from the most mainstream to the most obscure.

Rule #4: Diversifying risk across the audience funnel is key.
- Rented audiences offer rapid growth, but platform risk. 
- Owned audiences put you in control of your audience, but growth is slower. 
- And monetized audience is how you pay the bills, but you can’t monetize your audience without building trust.

Rule #5: Content channels & trends change but human psychology does not.
- Human beings are selfish. We selfishly do things that satisfy our most basic desire: survival. Survival in modern day society boils down to physical safety & psychological safety.

Rule #6: We are late stage on most content platforms.
- As platforms have entered the later innings of their life cycles, the quality bar for what is “worthy” of a consumer’s time continues to increase.

Rule #7: The tiktok-ification of media is almost complete.
- Every creator/brand is only as successful as its last post and it’s never been easier for someone with a small audience to get outsized results on a single piece of content.

Rule #8: Software is becoming content. 
- As the barriers to build software approach 0, software is a new content medium which can be used to build and own audience.

Rule #9: AI is a supporting actor in media. 
- The question to ask is not how much of this content is AI or human-generated. 
- It’s how well does this content resonate with its audience.

Rule #10: No content is original. 
- It’s all a remix of prior ideas that came before. Great artists steal, bad artists copy. Media companies should behave in the same manner.

Rule #11: A modern media company serves 3 customers
- Its audience, its creators, and those who pay the bills. 
- The product a media company offers to serve each of these customers can be/is likely different.

Rule #12: A media company is like an investor.
- Deploying resources based on the risk/return profile of an investment and the amount of resource required.
- Example: a book should start as a blog. A blog should start as an article. An article should start as a tweet.

comments.text:
What stands out to me is how consistently these failures trace back to operating discipline, not technical sophistication. AI doesn’t introduce new problems so much as it removes the buffer that used to hide them. Weak data ownership, unclear decision rights, slow governance, and misaligned incentives all existed before AI. The difference now is they surface immediately and at scale.
From a People and operating-model lens, the pilot graveyard, FUD, and talent gaps are tightly linked. Organizations try to “add” AI without redefining who decides what, how work flows, or how success is measured. Without that clarity, adoption stalls regardless of model quality.The takeaway I keep coming back to is that AI scales whatever system it lands in. If the system is coherent, you get leverage. If it’s fragmented, you get faster fragmentation. Fixing foundations first isn’t conservative. It’s the only way this becomes durable.

comments.text:
What stands out to me is how consistently these failures trace back to operating discipline, not technical sophistication. AI doesn’t introduce new problems so much as it removes the buffer that used to hide them. Weak data ownership, unclear decision rights, slow governance, and misaligned incentives all existed before AI. The difference now is they surface immediately and at scale.
From a People and operating-model lens, the pilot graveyard, FUD, and talent gaps are tightly linked. Organizations try to “add” AI without redefining who decides what, how work flows, or how success is measured. Without that clarity, adoption stalls regardless of model quality.The takeaway I keep coming back to is that AI scales whatever system it lands in. If the system is coherent, you get leverage. If it’s fragmented, you get faster fragmentation. Fixing foundations first isn’t conservative. It’s the only way this becomes durable.

We are currently working with a Fortune 10 company to find niche experts, as they realize their job is to hire experts, not find them. 

P.S- Acquiring small boutique firms is definitely a good option to explore to help accelerate your growth goals.

text:
I was drowning in interviews last week. 

30 hours of 15-minute calls. Back-to-back. No time for meals or getting any other work done. 

I knew it wasn't sustainable, so I used AI to let me take back control of my calendar with a tik-tok style hiring site. 

Here's how I built it...

The situation: we're hiring 100+ people this year and haven't brought on a FT recruiter yet. Which means until further notice, I'm our recruiter. 

Last week, I had 30 hours of interviews, many of which were info interviews with candidates who we did outreach to. I basically repeated the same script + Q&A in each interview. Educating prospects is necessary, but blowing up my calendar is not. 

The solve: standing up a TikTok-style hiring site that provides background on our company & the positions, and that we can add to as new FAQs come in from candidates. 

I spun up the hiring site on Lovable in 30 minutes with this process. 

Here's the prompt I used to complete 75% of the build:

I want to build a tiktok style site that i can use for hiring at tenex that i can send to interested candidates to learn more about our company and our roles.

I want a user to be able to swipe through videos (that answer different questions/topics) and i want a table of contents to the right of the videos so that if a user knows the topic/question they want to watch a video about they can just click and scroll straight to that topic.

I want to easily be able to add new videos/questions as needed.

For now you can put in placeholders for the topics/videos:

What is Tenex?
What is the long-term vision?
Who are our customers?
How big is the business?
What is our culture?
What are the hours?
What is the job of an AI Strategist?
What is the AI Strategist interview process?
How does AI Strategist compensation work?
What is the job of an AI Engineer?
What is the AI Engineer interview process?
How does AI Engineer compensation work?

We want a clean, minimal, and tasteful UI. Go online and find the hallmarks of AI generated user interfaces and front end code and avoid those at all costs. Create a clean clear and consistent minimal and modern user interface.

Miscellaneous items: 
- Add company logo to the app (attached)
- Store videos I upload in your cloud product
- Optimize the site for speed of loading
- Add a button for candidates to be able to apply directly from the site

3) They get to live at the frontier of AI, while tackling a variety of complex business problems.

If you want to work with engineers from NASA, Google, YC-backed startups and other high-talent density eng orgs, hit us up at tenex[.]co.

text:
My cofounder spends 50% of his time in interviews convincing candidates why not to join our company. 

I think it's genius & more founders should do it. 

He'll say things like: 
- "I was here until midnight last night. Someone is always here until 10pm."
- "A lot of the work is unsexy & mind-numbing."
- "If you don't think about your work in your free time, we're probably not the right co for you."
- "We do not believe in work life balance. That doesn't mean family & things aren't important. They are. But balance doesn't exist." 

This has absolutely caused candidates to pull out of the process. They concede that Tenex probably isn't the best fit for them. 

It's a bold strategy & invites short-term pain, but it is SOOOO much better than the alternative....

Someone quits 3 months in because they didn't truly appreciate what they were signing up for. 

They're burnt out & disenfranchised. 
We've spent 3 months developing/supporting talent. 
And we need to gracefully transition client work to a different eng. 

It's a mess. 

Now, are there a lot of redeeming qualities that make working at our company great? Ofc. 
- You're part of a massive mission, to build a modern-day Bell Labs. 
- You'll learn more here than anywhere. Guaranteed.
- You'll make a fuck ton of money (if you're good). 
- You'll work with the smartest, kindest, and most fun team of your life.

But we need you to say yes with the clearest of eyes to all of the shitiness that lies ahead.

p.s. s/o to my cofounder Arman Hezarkhani for the inspo. give him a follow.

text:
Pretty wild convo I just had with the Head of AI at a $50bn tech company. 

They're watching a massive class divide be created in real time before their eyes. 

60% of employees are AI-native. Use ChatGPT >20x per month. Constantly mining for ways to leverage AI in their workflows & internal tools. 

40% are AI-skeptics. Don't use an LLM as a daily driver. Try out an AI tool for 5 minutes, don't like the output, then complain that the technology creates slop. 

Previous technology waves didn't create the sort of intra-company productivity gap we're about to witness. 

The difference between the excel warrior using their mouse vs. memorized shortcuts is ~25%. 

The difference between an AI-native & AI-resistant knowledge worker will be 10-100x. And that gap is going to grow rapidly. 

It's every company's responsibility to (selfishly) get all of their employees on the right curve. 

And it's every knowledge worker's best defense against irrelevancy to embrace this technology as quickly as humanly possible. Living on the frontier is your only option.

Adoption theater isn’t the same thing as capability.

text:
Spent an hour with Alexander Berger from bolt.new. I wanted to figure out how teams are jumping over PRD culture + shipping features faster in the age of AI.

Here's the Alex² math:

3 weeks — how long your last idea took to become a doc, then mockups, then code, then shipped.

$47,000 — rough cost of a PRD cycle when you add up the salaries of everyone playing telephone with your idea. 

30 minutes — how long it can take to build a clickable prototype that shows exactly what you mean instead.

Alex's process:

 - pick one pixel you want to fix (not a whole product—one element)
 - right-click → Inspect → copy the HTML + styles
 - paste into Bolt (or Lovable, Replit, v0)
 - tell it to match everything exactly
 - add your change
 - send the link to your stakeholders, let it do the talking
-  annnndddd if you're building solo, nothing's stopping you from making a million-dollar company doing this process over and over again (the tradeoff is never building a product ever) 

Subscribe to ultrathink 👇

text:
AI "agent" is a word everyone uses, but most people have no idea what it means. 

I wanted to bring clarity to the term, so I asked my engineers how they would define an agent. 

Here are the best responses I got: 

1) A software program that uses AI to accomplish a roughly-defined task.
- Arman Hezarkhani

2) Systems where LLMs dynamically direct their own processes and tool usage, maintaining control over how they accomplish tasks. 
- Dan Zakon (h/t Anthropic)

3) The model is the brain, the harness is the set of tools and the loop that allows the model to be multi step, and agent is the model running inside the harness.
- CJ Hess
 
4) An AI agent is a framework combining information retrieval + LLM/VLM to serve broader objectives than a single VLM/LLM.
- Raghav Dixit

5) A system that works toward a goal across multiple steps, assessing its situation and adjusting its actions in response to new information.
- Jason Brown
 
What's your definition of an agent?

I'm floored that the vast minority of people I interview send thank you emails. Like 1-2 out of 10. 

Back when I was interviewing for jobs, it was one of the biggest faux pas to not send a thank you email. Like instant disqualification. 

Has conventional etiquette just changed? Is it just a generational thing? Very curious.

comments.text: I think it’s just a generational thing. That was one of the first things that I was taught to do.

author.occupation: Director of Brand Training

comments.text:
To me, a thank-you email is the minimum, and after 15 years in this industry, I can tell you it matters.

The market is tough. Companies will continue to lean out as AI makes teams more productive. I’m surprised how many people still overlook the value of standing out in simple, human ways.

Candidates have to differentiate. A few suggestions:

• Don’t send the same thank-you to everyone. Make it personal. Something should stand out about each person you meet. Note it during the interview and reference it later.

• Use the thank-you to reinforce your value or clarify anything you did not fully cover in the interview.

• Match the medium to the situation. In-office, consider a handwritten note. Remote, individual emails, short videos, or audio notes via LinkedIn all work.

When I left my first corporate role, I had two opportunities. What helped me stand out was writing handwritten notes to everyone I met, more than 10 people. I wrote them on the flight home, bundled them, and sent them via certified mail to the most senior leader.

When they received the package, it made an impression and sparked conversations about my interactions.

I got offers from both.

Sometimes the differentiator is not louder. It is more intentional.

text:
#ad My business 10x’d in one year. 

And it was one of the most challenging professional periods of my life.
 
You’ll understand why in a second, but I wish that I had Intuit Enterprise Suite (who I’ve partnered with for this video) acting as the backbone of our business during this period of hypergrowth. 

In 2019, Morning Brew grew from 100,000 subscribers to 1 million. 

And on the back of that growth, revenue jumped from $20 million ultimately to $70 million and our team went from 50 to 300 in just 24 months. 

Super exciting, right? Also incredibly stressful. 

During this period of hypergrowth things started to break. 

We went from onboarding 1 person a month to 10 people per month. 

Not only did we have to completely rebuild our onboarding & payroll processes from the ground up, but we also had to offer better benefits than our company’s dental policy being a bag of flossers. 

We also had to start thinking really hard about our finances. 

No more spreadsheets, no more passively following up on payments we were due. We were managing many millions of dollars of operating expenses a month and had 7-figures worth of account receivables at any given time. 

And lastly, I had to completely change how I spent my time as the CEO of an 8-figure business. I had to go from working in the business to working on the business. And I had to spend my time on things like goal-setting and managing our execs versus taking sales calls with advertisers. 

Reinventing myself as CEO was a full-time job in itself, which is why having something like Intuit Enterprise Suite to help navigate our growth across the business would have been invaluable to free up my time. 

From simplifying enterprise payroll & HR to accelerating AR and retaining top performers with benefits, Intuit enterprise Suite truly offers a rock solid foundation for growing an 8-figure business. 
It's the AI-native ERP that scales with your business.

comments.text:
I am normally a data guy, and while I don’t have metrics on this one, I’ve worked around creating operational efficiency long enough to know when something is really moving the needle. I also know this one isn’t as smooth or as pretty as other automated workflows I’ve created but it has been a big winner multiple times. 

Earlier this year, while working with a large SMB client, they had a major gap that made AI automations a pretty distant reality. Like many large SMBs and midsized companies, they didn’t have good SOPs. This large gap is a boat anchor on your business right now.

Solution: I had them record themselves doing their repeatable tasks, then took transcripts from that video, & then dumped the transcript into a custom GPT, that output a detailed SOP, which was a great first step. I then took that doc and pushed it into another custom GPT, that then output an automation tool specific (ie n8n) process document to detail & scope out what was needed for the specific workflow automation to be built, for a new automation builder. 

Was it perfect, nope! But it filled that enormous gap at about 85-95%, & allowed them to start creating successful AI Automations. I’ve used it w/ multiple companies now, w/ similar success.

text:
Prototyping is not the future.

It’s how business has always worked.

My grandfather built products by making them, showing them, and refining them.

(You can thank him for those toothpaste squeezers.)

But, I’m willing to bet “show and tell” hasn’t advanced this far since cave paintings.

Code, demos, and design can now be shown almost instantly—not explained.

Vibe coding works when you can’t afford to guess.

Because if time is money, why debate hypotheticals when you can demo reality?

This is how Google has shipped much of what it’s built over the past year.

We wrote a full field guide on talking prototypes, micro tools, and apps into existence w/ Gemini 3. 

Thanks to Logan Kilpatrick for talking me through this playbook 👇

text:
Everyone said 2025 was the year of AI agents.

It wasn’t.

We’re not even close.

What actually happened?

Companies gave ChatGPT access to the team, fired people expecting “efficiency,” but skipped the hard part (aka rebuilding workflows, and then blamed the tech when shit hit the fan.

I’ve seen this playbook 100x, and it doesn’t work.

Here’s what does:

Embracing the slog.
Treating AI implementation like onboarding a junior hire.
Dedicating full-time resourcing to rebuild process, NOT just testing tools.

Most orgs are stuck in Phase 1 of a 4-phase journey:
1) Single-player tools
2) Single-player processes
3) Multiplayer, single-function
4) Multiplayer, cross-functional

Everyone wants Phase 4. Nobody wants to do Phase 2.

At Tenex, we spent hundreds of hours helping one client rebuild their outbound SDR motion to make it AI-native. Took months. It was brutal.

But it lead to 3x the lead volume and 5x the response rate. 

So here’s my 2026 prediction: The winners aren’t the ones with the flashiest AI product.
Companies that dedicate full-time resources to rebuilding specific processes will be poised to see 10x gains.

text:
I built a Client Radar that will—no exaggeration—make my business millions.

It solves a problem I've had across all of my companies. 

How do we play offense with customers as our business scales and things more easily slip through the cracks? 

- That means identifying cracks early before churn becomes inevitable. 
- That means mining for expansion opportunities proactively. 

So I built an AI agent in Zapier that scans our company's...

- Slack messages
- Notion meeting transcripts
- Gmail threads

And transforms them into a weekly customer sentiment analysis report that provides the following: 

1) Relationship health by client
- Sentiment score (X/10)
- Communication volume (# of messages exchanged) 
- Average response time
- Emotional indicators
- Evidence quotes 
- Relationship trending up/down
- Churn probability
- Recommended action

2) Client crisis intervention (for health scores below 5)
- Who owns comms
- Timeline for intervention
- Proposed script
- Desired outcome

3) Strategic initiatives (for account growth) 
- The client
- The growth opportunity
- Proposed comms with the client

4) Comprehensive customer dashboard
- Health score distribution (% excellent, good, needs attention, at risk)
- Churn risk assessment (low risk, medium risk, high risk) 
- Resource allocation (how to focus employee time by account) 
- High-level strategic recommendations

This may be the highest ROI workflow I've built to date & I'd love for you to put it to work in your business as well.

text:
This is our entire bet at Tenex. 

AI is a generational technology, yet the journey from AI-absent to AI-native for companies of all sizes will be painful. 

Getting an individual to start using ChatGPT is easy. 

Rebuilding full processes/workflows in a company is exceptionally difficult. And the bigger the company, the harder it gets. 

Software co's are going to do the bare minimum to invest in enablement, because that's not their business. 

And traditional consultancies, don't have the density of AI-native talent to properly solve this problem. 

Which leaves a gaping hole (like global GDP gaping) for a number of companies to help shepherd this new era of technology & help businesses fight irrelevancy.

text:
I am so damn grateful for entrepreneurship. 

But not for the reasons you might expect. 

Yes, this line of work is a gift for a certain kind of crazy. 

It offers financial freedom to those with the stomach for it. It offers an intellectual high for those obsessed with navigating the idea maze. It offers autonomy to those who couldn't imagine having a boss. It offers purpose for those who yearn for mission & impact. 

And yet, that's not the part I'm most indebted to. 

Entrepreneurship is personal growth disguised as professional growth, and as I reflect on 10 years of building, that is the part I'm in awe of. 

Building a business is like holding a funhouse mirror to your face 24/7. 

It accentuates your zone of genius. For me, that's curiosity, playfulness, and default optimism. 

But it also makes you face the ugly in your life. 
- Insecurity around my ability to focus
- Struggles with process & detail
- Addiction to technology & difficulty being truly present

So if you tune into the journey as the ultimate lever for reaching your personal potential, professional success will be a welcome consolation prize.

comments.text: Absolutely, bro, entrepreneurship is the mirror that forces growth and self-mastery.
